prompt:
A *numerical semigroup* is a set $S\subseteq\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that contains $0$, is closed under addition (if $x,y\in S$ then $x+y\in S$), and contains all but finitely many nonnegative integers. For positive integers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ with $\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_n)=1$, $\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle=\{c_1a_1+\cdots+c_na_n\mid c_i\in\mathbb N_0\}$ is the semigroup *generated* by $a_1,\dots,a_n$; for example $\langle4,6,9\rangle=\{0,4,6,8,9,10,12,13,\dots\}$ contains all integers after $12$.

(i) Compute all elements of $\langle5,7,11,16\rangle$.
(ii) Can this numerical semigroup be generated by a set of fewer than $4$ integers? Prove your answer.
(iii) Compute all elements of $\langle3,7,8\rangle$.
(iv) Can this numerical semigroup be generated by a set of fewer than $3$ integers? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Compute and compare
solutions.body:
(i) Sums of $5,7,11,16$ below $15$: $0,5,7,10,11,12,14$ (e.g. $12=5+7$, $14=7+7$); the numbers $1,2,3,4,6,8,9,13$ cannot be formed (for $13$: $13-5=8$, $13-7=6$, $13-11=2$ are not in the semigroup). Also $15=5\cdot3$, $16$, $17=5+5+7$, $18=7+11$, $19=5+7+7$ are in, and adding $5$ repeatedly gives every $n\ge15$.

(ii) Yes: $16=5+11$, so any use of $16$ can be replaced by $5$ and $11$, hence $\langle5,7,11,16\rangle=\langle5,7,11\rangle$.

(iii) $0,3,6,7,8$ are in. The numbers $1,2,4,5$ are not: they are below $7$ and are not multiples of $3$. Next $9=3\cdot3$, $10=3+7$, $11=3+8$, and adding $3$ repeatedly gives all $n\ge9$.

(iv) No. A generating set with one element and gcd $1$ is $\{1\}$, giving $\mathbb N_0$, so suppose $\langle3,7,8\rangle=\langle a,b\rangle$ with $a<b$. The smallest positive element of $\langle a,b\rangle$ is $a$, so $a=3$. The elements of $\langle3,b\rangle$ below $b$ are multiples of $3$, so the smallest non-multiple of $3$ in the semigroup is $b$; in $\langle3,7,8\rangle$ it is $7$, so $b=7$. But $8\notin\langle3,7\rangle=\{0,3,6,7,9,10,\dots\}$, a contradiction.

solutions.title: Add the coefficients
solutions.body: Write $x=\sum c_ia_i$ and $y=\sum d_ia_i$ with $c_i,d_i\in\mathbb N_0$. Then $x+y=\sum(c_i+d_i)a_i$ with $c_i+d_i\in\mathbb N_0$, so $x+y\in\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle$. ∎

Prove that $\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle$ contains all but a finite number of the nonnegative integers. (Hint: you may use without proof that if $\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_n)=1$, there are possibly negative integers $d_1,\dots,d_n$ with $d_1a_1+\cdots+d_na_n=1$.)
answer: Every integer $\ge s=a_1\sum a_i\,M$ (with $M=\max|d_i|$) is in the semigroup.

solutions.title: Bezout and a large shift
solutions.body:
Let $d_1a_1+\cdots+d_na_n=1$ and $M=\max|d_i|$. Put $s=a_1M(a_1+\cdots+a_n)$. For $0\le r<a_1$,
$$s+r=\sum_{i}(a_1M+rd_i)a_i,$$
and $|rd_i|\le(a_1-1)M<a_1M$, so every coefficient $a_1M+rd_i$ is positive. Hence $s+r\in\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle$.

Now let $x\ge s$ and write $x-s=qa_1+r$ with $0\le r<a_1$, $q\ge0$. Then $x=qa_1+(s+r)$ is the sum of two elements of the semigroup, so $x\in\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle$. So only integers below $s$ can be missing. ∎

Prove that any numerical semigroup $S$ (second definition: contains $0$, closed under addition, contains all but finitely many nonnegative integers) is generated by a finite set $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ of positive integers with $\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_n)=1$, i.e. $S=\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle$.
answer: $S$ is generated by the finite set $S\cap[1,F+m]$.

solutions.title: Finite generating set
solutions.body:
Let $F$ be the largest integer not in $S$ (if $S=\mathbb N_0$, take $\{1\}$) and $m$ the smallest positive element of $S$. Let $B=S\cap[1,F+m]$, a finite set. Clearly $\langle B\rangle\subseteq S$ by closure under addition.

Conversely we show $x\in S\Rightarrow x\in\langle B\rangle$ by induction on $x$. For $x=0$ it is empty sum. If $1\le x\le F+m$ then $x\in B$. If $x>F+m$ then $x-m>F$, so $x-m\in S$ and is smaller; by induction $x-m\in\langle B\rangle$ and $m\in B$, so $x\in\langle B\rangle$.

gcd: if $m=1$ then $1\in B$. Otherwise $m\ge2$ and $F+1,F+2\le F+m$ are both greater than $F$, hence in $S$ and in $B$, and $\gcd(F+1,F+2)=1$. So $\gcd(B)=1$. ∎

We say that $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ is a *minimal generating set* of $S$ if $S$ is generated by $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ and $S$ cannot be generated by any set of positive integers with fewer than $n$ elements. Prove that every numerical semigroup $S$ has a unique minimal generating set.
answer: The unique minimal generating set is the set of positive elements of $S$ that are not a sum of two positive elements of $S$.

solutions.title: Irreducible elements
solutions.body:
Call a positive $x\in S$ *irreducible* if it is not a sum $u+v$ of two positive elements of $S$, and let $G$ be the set of irreducibles.

$G$ is finite: if $x>F+m$ then $x=(x-m)+m$ with $x-m>F$ positive in $S$, so $x$ is reducible; thus $G\subseteq[1,F+m]$.

$G$ generates $S$: by strong induction every positive $x\in S$ is a sum of irreducibles (either $x$ is irreducible, or $x=u+v$ with smaller positive $u,v\in S$).

Every generating set $A$ of $S$ (positive integers) contains $G$: if $g\in G$ is written $g=\sum c_ia_i$ with $a_i\in A\subseteq S$, then having two or more summands would split $g$ into two positive elements of $S$; so $g$ equals a single $a_i\in A$.

Hence any generating set has at least $|G|$ elements, and $G$ itself has exactly $|G|$. A generating set of size $|G|$ contains $G$ and so equals $G$. Therefore $G$ is the unique minimal generating set. ∎

solutions.title: Pairing argument
solutions.body: Let $N=F(S)$. If $N=-1$ then $S=\mathbb N_0$, $g=0$ and the claim $-1\le-1$ holds. Otherwise $N\ge1$ is a gap. For each $i$ with $1\le i<N/2$, at least one of $i,N-i$ is a gap (else $N=i+(N-i)\in S$); if $N$ is even, $N/2$ is a gap (else $N=\frac N2+\frac N2\in S$). The sets $\{N\}$, $\{i,N-i\}$ for $1\le i<N/2$, and $\{N/2\}$ (for even $N$) are disjoint and each contains a gap. Their number is $\frac{N+1}2$ for odd $N$ and $\frac N2+1$ for even $N$; in both cases at least $\frac{N+1}2$. So $g\ge\frac{N+1}2$, i.e. $F(S)=N\le2g-1$. ∎

prompt: The Chicken McNugget Theorem states that if McDonald's sells Chicken McNuggets in boxes of $a$ or $b$ McNuggets with $\gcd(a,b)=1$, then the largest number of McNuggets one cannot buy is $ab-a-b$. Restate this in terms of the numerical semigroup $\langle a,b\rangle$ (whose Frobenius number $F(S)$ is the largest integer not in $S$).

solutions.title: Restatement
solutions.body: The numbers of McNuggets one can buy are exactly the elements of $\langle a,b\rangle$, so the theorem says that the Frobenius number is $F(\langle a,b\rangle)=ab-a-b$.

prompt: Let $a,b$ be coprime positive integers and $S=\langle a,b\rangle$. Prove the Chicken McNugget Theorem: the largest integer not in $S$ is $ab-a-b$. (Possible hint: write the numbers $1,\dots,ab$ in a grid with rows $1..a$, $a+1..2a$, ... and cross out the ones you can buy.)

solutions.title: Unique representation
solutions.body:
Every integer $N$ can be written uniquely as $N=xa+yb$ with $x\in\mathbb Z$ and $0\le y\le a-1$: existence because $\gcd(a,b)=1$ gives some solution and $y$ can be reduced mod $a$ (replace $(x,y)$ by $(x+bt,y-at)$); uniqueness because $yb\equiv y'b\pmod a$ forces $y\equiv y'\pmod a$.

$N\in S$ iff $x\ge0$ in this representation: if $N=x'a+y'b$ with $x',y'\ge0$, write $y'=ta+y$ with $0\le y<a$, $t\ge0$; then $N=(x'+tb)a+yb$, so by uniqueness $x=x'+tb\ge0$. Conversely $x\ge0$ and $y\ge0$ give a representation.

The number $ab-a-b=(-1)a+(a-1)b$ has $x=-1<0$, so it is not in $S$. If $N>ab-a-b$ and $x\le-1$, then $N=xa+yb\le-a+(a-1)b=ab-a-b$, a contradiction; so $x\ge0$ and $N\in S$. Hence the largest non-element is $ab-a-b$. ∎

prompt: Let $a,b$ be coprime positive integers and $S=\langle a,b\rangle$. The *genus* of $S$ is the number of positive integers not in $S$. Find, with proof, the genus of $\langle a,b\rangle$.

solutions.title: Symmetry about $F/2$
solutions.body:
Let $F=ab-a-b$, the largest gap. Write each integer uniquely as $N=xa+yb$, $0\le y\le a-1$; recall $N\in S\iff x\ge0$. For $N=xa+yb$ we get $F-N=(-x-1)a+(a-1-y)b$ with $0\le a-1-y\le a-1$, which is the unique representation of $F-N$. So $F-N\in S\iff -x-1\ge0\iff x<0\iff N\notin S$.

Thus among the integers $0,1,\dots,F$ paired as $N\leftrightarrow F-N$, in each pair exactly one lies in $S$ (the pairing has no fixed point since $N=F-N$ would put $N$ both in and out of $S$). So exactly half of the $F+1$ integers $0,\dots,F$ are not in $S$, and no integer above $F$ is missing. Hence the genus is $\frac{F+1}2=\frac{ab-a-b+1}2=\frac{(a-1)(b-1)}2$. ∎

solutions.title: Counting by residue classes
solutions.body: For $i=1,\dots,a-1$ write $ib=q_ia+r_i$ with $0<r_i<a$; the $r_i$ are a permutation of $1,\dots,a-1$. The smallest element of $S$ congruent to $ib$ mod $a$ is $ib$ (any $xa+yb\equiv ib$ forces $y\equiv i\pmod a$, so $y\ge i$). So in residue class $r_i$ the gaps are $r_i,r_i+a,\dots,r_i+(q_i-1)a$: $q_i$ gaps. Summing $ib=q_ia+r_i$ over $i$: $b\frac{a(a-1)}2=a\sum q_i+\frac{a(a-1)}2$, so $\sum q_i=\frac{(a-1)(b-1)}2$. ∎

solutions.title: Define $S$ and check minimality in each class
solutions.body:
Let $w_i=k_im+i$ and $S=\langle m,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}\rangle$ (it is cofinite: $S$ contains $w_i+cm$ for every $c\ge0$ and every $i$, and all multiples of $m$, hence every integer $\ge\max_iw_i$, so it is a numerical semigroup). $S$ contains $m$ and no positive integer below $m$, so its multiplicity is $m$. By the characterisation of the Ap\'ery set it suffices to show that $w_i$ is the smallest element of $S$ congruent to $i$.

Let $x\in S$ with $x\equiv i\pmod m$, $x=w_{j_1}+\cdots+w_{j_n}+cm$ with $1\le j_t\le m-1$ and $c\ge0$ (if $x$ is not a multiple of $m$ there is at least one $w$). solutions.title: All $k_i\in\{1,2\}$
solutions.body:
$F<2m$ means $(k_i-1)m+i<2m$ for all $i$. If some $k_i\ge3$ then $(k_i-1)m+i\ge2m+1$, violating it; if all $k_i\le2$, then $(k_i-1)m+i\le m+i<2m$. So the condition is exactly $k_i\in\{1,2\}$ for all $i$.

Any such sequence is a valid Ap\'ery sequence: $k_i+k_j\ge2\ge k_{i+j}$ and $k_i+k_j+1\ge3\ge k_{i+j-m}$. Genus $g=\sum k_i$ means exactly $g-(m-1)$ of the $m-1$ coefficients equal $2$ and the rest equal $1$. Different sequences give different semigroups, so the number is $\binom{m-1}{g-m+1}$ (zero if $g-m+1$ is outside $[0,m-1]$). ∎

Substituting $m'=m-1$ in the first part gives $\sum_{m'}\binom{m'-1}{(g-1)-m'+1}=N_{g-1}$, and substituting $m'=m-1$ in the second gives $\sum_{m'}\binom{m'-1}{(g-2)-m'+1}=N_{g-2}$. solutions.title: Irreducibility of the Ap\'ery generators
solutions.body:
The minimal generating set of $S$ consists of the irreducible positive elements of $S$ (positive elements that are not a sum of two positive elements of $S$). By the Ap\'ery description it is contained in $\{m,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}\}$ with $w_i=k_im+i$; $m$ is always irreducible. So $S$ is MED iff every $w_i$ is irreducible.

Suppose $w_i=u+v$ with $u,v\in S$ positive. Neither can be a multiple of $m$ (if $u=cm$ then $v=w_i-cm\in S$ is smaller than $w_i$ in the class of $i$, contradiction). So $u\equiv j$, $v\equiv j'\pmod m$ with $j,j'\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}$, hence $u\ge w_j$, $v\ge w_{j'}$ and $w_i=u+v\ge w_j+w_{j'}\ge w_i$ (the last because $w_j+w_{j'}\in S$ lies in the class of $i$). So $u=w_j$, $v=w_{j'}$ and $w_i=w_j+w_{j'}$. Conversely such an equation makes $w_i$ reducible.

$w_j+w_{j'}=(k_j+k_{j'})m+j+j'$. With $j+j'\equiv i$: if $j+j'=i<m$, equality $w_i=w_j+w_{j'}$ means $k_i=k_j+k_{j'}$; if $j+j'=i+m$, it means $k_i=k_j+k_{j'}+1$. solutions.title: Validity
solutions.body: Let $S$ be a numerical semigroup and $n$ a generator of $S$. Then $S\setminus\{n\}$ contains $0$ and is cofinite. It is closed under addition: if $u,v\in S\setminus\{n\}$ and $u+v=n$, then neither $u$ nor $v$ is $0$ would make $n$ a sum of two positive elements of $S$, contradicting that $n$ is a generator; and if one of them is $0$ then $u+v\in S\setminus\{n\}$ trivially. solutions.title: Every semigroup appears exactly once
solutions.body:
Let $S$ have gaps $a_1<\dots<a_g$ and put $S_i=\mathbb N_0\setminus\{a_1,\dots,a_i\}$, so $S_0=\mathbb N_0$ and $S_g=S$. We claim $S_i$ is a child of $S_{i-1}$. Here $F(S_{i-1})=a_{i-1}<a_i$. Is $a_i$ a generator of $S_{i-1}$? Write $ib=q_ia+r_i$, $0<r_i<a$ for $1\le i\le a-1$; then the $r_i$ are a permutation of $1,\dots,a-1$ and $k_{r_i}=q_i$ (the least element of the class $r_i$ is $q_ia+r_i$). The gaps in class $r_i$ are $r_i,r_i+a,\dots,r_i+(q_i-1)a$, with sum $q_ir_i+a\frac{q_i(q_i-1)}2$.

The weight is $W=\sum_{i=1}^{a-1}\left(q_ir_i+\frac a2q_i^2-\frac a2q_i\right)=\frac12\sum(aq_i^2+2q_ir_i)-\frac a2\sum q_i$.

solutions.title: Evaluate the sums
solutions.body:
Summing $ib=q_ia+r_i$ gives $b\frac{a(a-1)}2=a\sum q_i+\frac{a(a-1)}2$, so $\sum q_i=\frac{(a-1)(b-1)}2$. Squaring, $b^2i^2=a^2q_i^2+2aq_ir_i+r_i^2$; summing over $i$ and using $\sum r_i^2=\sum i^2=\frac{(a-1)a(2a-1)}6$:
$$a\sum(aq_i^2+2q_ir_i)=(b^2-1)\frac{(a-1)a(2a-1)}6,\quad\text{so}\quad\sum(aq_i^2+2q_ir_i)=\frac{(b^2-1)(a-1)(2a-1)}6.$$
Therefore $W=\frac{(b^2-1)(a-1)(2a-1)}{12}-\frac{a(a-1)(b-1)}4=\frac{(a-1)(b-1)\left[(b+1)(2a-1)-3a\right]}{12}=\frac{(a-1)(b-1)(2ab-a-b-1)}{12}$. ∎ (Check: $\langle3,7\rangle$ has gaps $1,2,4,5,8,11$: weight $31=\frac{2\cdot6\cdot32}{12}\cdot\ldots$ and $\langle3,7\rangle$: $(2)(6)(42-11)/12=31$ ✓.)

prompt:
A *numerical semigroup* is a set $S\subseteq\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that contains $0$, is closed under addition, and contains all but finitely many nonnegative integers. Its *genus* $g(S)$ is the number of positive integers not in $S$ (the *gaps*), its *Frobenius number* $F(S)$ is the largest gap ($F=-1$ if $S=\mathbb N_0$), and its *multiplicity* $m(S)$ is the smallest positive element. The *generators* of $S$ are the elements of its (unique) minimal generating set, i.e. the positive elements that are not a sum of two positive elements of $S$; the *embedding dimension* $e(S)$ is their number.

Let $p(x,y,z)$ be the number of partitions of $x$ into at most $y$ parts, each of size at most $z$. Prove that the number of numerical semigroups with genus $g$, multiplicity $m$ and weight excess $w$ satisfying $m<F<2m$ is exactly $p\big(w-(g-m+1),\ g-m+1,\ 2m-2-g\big)$.

(Here $w$ is the weight in excess of the minimum for genus $g$: $w=(\text{sum of the gaps})-(1+2+\cdots+g)$. This is the convention of the official solution; with the plain sum of the gaps the statement fails, e.g. for $\langle2,5\rangle$ with $g=2$, $m=2$.)
answer: Semigroups with $m<F<2m$ correspond to $t=g-m+1$ element subsets $\{i_1<\dots<i_t\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,m-1\}$, with $w-t=\sum(i_a-a)$.

solutions.title: Describe the semigroups
solutions.body:
Let $S$ have genus $g$, multiplicity $m$ and $m<F<2m$. Its gaps are $1,\dots,m-1$ and, since $m\in S$ and $F<2m$, further gaps of the form $m+i$ with $i\in I$ for some nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,m-1\}$ ($F>m$ forces $I\ne\emptyset$). So $g=(m-1)+|I|$, i.e. $|I|=t:=g-m+1$.

Conversely, for any nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,m-1\}$ the set $S=\mathbb N_0\setminus(\{1,\dots,m-1\}\cup\{m+i:i\in I\})$ is a numerical semigroup: it contains $0$ and all $n\ge2m$, and the sum of two positive elements is at least $2m$ (the smallest positive element is $m$). It has multiplicity $m$ and $F=m+\max I\in(m,2m)$. So these semigroups correspond bijectively to $t$-element subsets $I=\{i_1<\dots<i_t\}$ of $\{1,\dots,m-1\}$.

solutions.title: Weight and partitions
solutions.body:
The sum of the gaps is $\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}j+\sum_{a=1}^t(m+i_a)$, while $1+\dots+g=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}j+\sum_{a=1}^t(m-1+a)$. Hence $w=\sum_{a=1}^t(i_a-a+1)$, i.e. $w-t=\sum_{a=1}^t(i_a-a)$.

Put $\lambda_a=i_a-a$. Since $1\le i_1<\dots<i_t\le m-1$ are integers, $0\le\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_t\le m-1-t=2m-2-g$; conversely every such sequence gives a valid $I$ via $i_a=\lambda_a+a$. Discarding zeros, such sequences are exactly the partitions of $w-t$ into at most $t$ parts, each at most $2m-2-g$. Hence the number of semigroups is $p(w-t,t,2m-2-g)$ with $t=g-m+1$. ∎ (A computer enumeration of all semigroups of genus up to $9$ confirms this with $w$ the weight excess.)

prompt:
A *numerical semigroup* is a set $S\subseteq\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that contains $0$, is closed under addition, and contains all but finitely many nonnegative integers. Its *genus* $g(S)$ is the number of positive integers not in $S$ (the *gaps*), its *Frobenius number* $F(S)$ is the largest gap ($F=-1$ if $S=\mathbb N_0$), and its *multiplicity* $m(S)$ is the smallest positive element. The *generators* of $S$ are the elements of its (unique) minimal generating set, i.e. the positive elements that are not a sum of two positive elements of $S$; the *embedding dimension* $e(S)$ is their number.

A *partition* of a positive integer $n$ is a list $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_k$ of positive integers with sum $n$. The *Ferrers-Young diagram* of $\lambda$ has a row of $\lambda_1$ boxes, below it a left-aligned row of $\lambda_2$ boxes, and so on. The *hook* of a box consists of that box, the boxes to its right in its row and the boxes below it in its column; its length is the number of boxes. The *hookset* $H_\lambda$ is the set of hook lengths of $\lambda$ (for $5+3+2$ the hook lengths are $7,6,4,2,1$ in the first row, $4,3,1$ in the second, $2,1$ in the third, so $H_\lambda=\{1,2,3,4,6,7\}$).

Prove that for any partition $\lambda$, the set $\mathbb N_0\setminus H_\lambda$ is a numerical semigroup. (Possible hint: walk along the lower-right boundary of the diagram, from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner.)
answer: $\mathbb N_0\setminus H_\lambda$ contains $0$, is cofinite, and is closed under addition.

solutions.title: Boundary walk
solutions.body:
Walk along the lower-right boundary of the diagram from its bottom-left corner to its top-right corner. The walk consists of unit steps R (right) and U (up); number the steps $0,1,\dots,N$. The first step is R and the last is U. Each box corresponds to a pair (an R step $h$ under its column, a U step $u$ at the right end of its row) with $h$ before $u$, and the hook length of the box is $\text{pos}(u)-\text{pos}(h)$ (the steps strictly after $h$ up to and including $u$ are: the R steps under the boxes to the right of the box, and the U steps at the ends of the rows from its row down to the bottom of its column; their number is the arm plus the leg plus $1$). Every such pair of an R step followed later by a U step arises from a box. So $H_\lambda=\{j-i: \text{step } i\text{ is R, step } j\text{ is U}, i<j\}$.

Now $0\notin H_\lambda$ (hooks have length $\ge1$), and $H_\lambda\subseteq[1,N]$ so $\mathbb N_0\setminus H_\lambda$ is cofinite. For closure under addition, suppose $a,b\notin H_\lambda$ but $a+b\in H_\lambda$: there is an R step at $i$ and a U step at $i+a+b$. Step $i+a$ cannot be U (then $(i,i+a)$ would give a hook of length $a$), so it is R; but then $(i+a,i+a+b)$ is an R followed by a U at distance $b$, a hook of length $b$, a contradiction. (Cases $a=0$ or $b=0$ are trivial.) Hence $\mathbb N_0\setminus H_\lambda$ is closed under addition. ∎

solutions.title: Construct the boundary path
solutions.body:
Let the gaps of $S$ be $n_1<\dots<n_g$ (if $g=0$ take the empty partition). Consider the walk with steps numbered $0,\dots,n_g$ having a U at steps $n_1,\dots,n_g$ and an R at all other steps. It starts with R (as $0\in S$ is not a gap) and ends with U, so it is the lower-right boundary of a unique Ferrers-Young diagram of some partition $\lambda$, and by the previous part $H_\lambda=\{j-i: i<j,\ \text{R at }i,\ \text{U at }j\}$.

Each $n_k\in H_\lambda$: pair the R at step $0$ with the U at step $n_k$. Conversely suppose $j-i=a\in H_\lambda$ with R at $i$ and U at $j$. Then $j$ is a gap and $i$ is not a gap, so $i\in S$. If $a\in S$ then $j=i+a\in S$, a contradiction. So $a\notin S$, i.e. $a$ is a gap. Hence $H_\lambda$ is exactly the set of gaps of $S$. ∎
